question: According to the Foreword, what share of the world's population lived in extreme poverty in 1990 and what share lived in it in 2020?

results.source: Poverty, Prosperity and Planet Report 2026 - Overview.pdf
results.text:
Foreword
Decades of remarkable progress against poverty and inequality have given way to a period of slower and more uneven gains. Between 1990 and 2020, the share of the world's population living in extreme poverty fell from 43 percent to 11 percent, driven largely by gains in large middle-income economies. The number of economies with high inequality, measured by a Gini index above 40, declined from 70 in 2000 to 42 in 2024. But progress has slowed, and extreme poverty is increasingly concentrated in a few economies, most of them in Sub-Saharan Africa and in fragile and conflict-affected situations.

results.source: Poverty, Prosperity and Planet Report 2026 - Overview.pdf
results.text:
Overview
The reduction in global poverty over the past generation ranks among the great global achievements of economic development in the postwar era. In 1990, 43 percent of the world's population was living in extreme poverty. By 2020, the share was about 11 percent, and, now, more than two-thirds of humanity is living in economies in which extreme poverty has effectively ended, up from a fifth in 2000. This achievement is the standard against which the present situation must be measured, and the present falls short. Progress against extreme poverty has come to a standstill.

results.source: Poverty, Prosperity and Planet Report 2026 - Overview.pdf
results.text:

In 2026, an estimated 811 million people, 1 in 10, live below the international extreme poverty line of $3.00 a day, a rate unchanged since 2019. Without faster growth, the number will rise as populations grow more quickly where poverty is highest.

Overview
After rising during the COVID pandemic and then recovering, the extreme poverty rate has remained essentially unchanged. question: What is the number of people living on less than $8.30 a day, and what share of humanity is that?

results.source: Poverty, Prosperity and Planet Report 2026 - Overview.pdf
results.text:
Overview
The picture is different at higher poverty lines. At $4.20 and $8.30 a day (the standards typical of lower-middle- and upper-middle-income economies), poverty reduction has broadly maintained the earlier pace. Even so, nearly half of humanity-3.7 billion people-are still living on less than $8.30 a day. The share has fallen modestly, but population growth has offset much of the gain, keeping the absolute number stubbornly high.

results.source: Poverty, Prosperity and Planet Report 2026 - Overview.pdf
results.text:
Poverty
3. Escaping extreme poverty has not meant reaching the middle class. Nearly half of humanity, 3.7 billion people, is still living on less than $8.30 a day, the poverty line in upper-middle- income economies. Most people who have left extreme poverty since 2000 have moved only into the $3.00-$8.30 band: no longer extremely poor, but not economically secure, and one shock away from falling back into extreme poverty.

results.source: Poverty, Prosperity and Planet Report 2026 - Overview.pdf
results.text:
Tracking the global path to ending extreme poverty, with jobs at the center
On prosperity, most people who have escaped extreme poverty have not reached the middle class, and nearly half of humanity is still living on less than $8.30 a day and remain vulnerable to falling back. Fewer economies are now highly unequal, but the share of the world's people living in these economies has not fallen, and the closing of the Global Prosperity Gap has slowed to a fraction of the earlier pace. On the planet, climate risk is reaching people far above the poverty line: while emissions are growing in economies where the poor do not live, ending extreme poverty would add little to global emissions.

question: How many people are exposed to climate hazards but lack the means to cope with them, and where do most of them live relative to the extreme poverty line?

results.source: Poverty, Prosperity and Planet Report 2026 - Overview.pdf
results.text:
Foreword
Escaping extreme poverty does not guarantee economic security. Nearly half of humanity, 3.7 billion people, live below the $8.30-a-day poverty line typically used to measure poverty in upper-middle-income countries, leaving many vulnerable to falling back into extreme poverty after a shock. Weather-related shocks add to this vulnerability: 1.5 billion people, most living above the extreme poverty line, are exposed to climate hazards but lack the means to cope with these hazards. At the same time, the growth needed to end extreme poverty in the poorest countries would add little to global emissions.

results.source: Poverty, Prosperity and Planet Report 2026 - Overview.pdf
results.text:
Planet
6. Climate risk reaches well beyond the poor. Of the 4.6 billion people exposed to a major climate hazard, 1.5 billion are also highly vulnerable because they lack social protection or access to basic infrastructure, and most of the highly vulnerable live above the extreme poverty line. The risk is concentrated in the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan, and Pakistan and the Sub-Saharan Africa regions, where nearly half and over a third of the population, respectively, are at high risk, and almost everyone who is exposed is also vulnerable.

results.source: Poverty, Prosperity and Planet Report 2026 - Overview.pdf
results.text:
Deprivations extend beyond monetary measures: A deteriorating planet threatens the gains against poverty
Around 4.6 billion people live in exposed areas, and 2.7 billion live in highly vulnerable conditions; about 1.5 billion people experience both types of vulnerability. The drivers of multidimensional poverty also drive climate vulnerability. The same lack of schooling and missing infrastructure that identify a household as multidimensionally poor can convert a flood or a drought from a hazard into a catastrophe.

question: How did the number of high-inequality economies (Gini above 40) change between 2000 and 2024?

results.source: Poverty, Prosperity and Planet Report 2026 - Overview.pdf
results.text:
Prosperity
4. High inequality is retreating across economies but persists across people. The number of economies with a Gini index above 40 fell from 70 in 2000 to 42 in 2024, and those economies still above the threshold cut their average Gini from 51 to 46. Nonetheless, one in five people worldwide is still living in a high-inequality economy, a share unchanged since 2013 (refer to figure 2, panel a), and 37 economies have never left the above-40 group in 25 years. The concentration of the extreme poor is happening here, too. The share in high-inequality economies nearly doubled, to 36 percent.

results.source: Poverty, Prosperity and Planet Report 2026 - Overview.pdf
results.text: The report's count of high-inequality economies illustrates what a headline figure may conceal. The count fell from 70 in 2000 to 42 in 2024, a decline of more than one-third. Underlying this trend, the report's fresh duration analysis reveals two findings that emphasize the stubborn persistence of inequality. In 2000-24, the Gini index never rose above 40 in 79 economies and never fell below 40 in 37 economies. The middle is thin. Few economies spent between 5 and 20 years above the threshold before falling below the threshold. High inequality is apparently not a transitory state through which economies pass. It is a chronic condition either avoided or endured for decades.

5. The Prosperity Gap halved and then stalled. In 1990, incomes worldwide needed to rise 10.5-fold, on average, to reach the $28.00-a-person-a-day prosperity standard. By 2013, the Prosperity Gap had fallen to 5.5, and it stood at 4.5 in 2026 (refer to figure 2, panel b, left panel). Almost all the progress occurred before 2013. Over the latest decade, the gap has narrowed by only about 1.2 percent a year (refer to figure 2, panel b, right panel). The gap in Sub-Saharan Africa is at 11.1, twice the global average and roughly where the world stood in 1990.

question: Of the people exposed to a major climate hazard, how many are also highly vulnerable because they lack social protection or basic infrastructure?

results.source: Poverty, Prosperity and Planet Report 2026 - Overview.pdf
results.text:
Planet
6. Climate risk reaches well beyond the poor. Of the 4.6 billion people exposed to a major climate hazard, 1.5 billion are also highly vulnerable because they lack social protection or access to basic infrastructure, and most of the highly vulnerable live above the extreme poverty line. The risk is concentrated in the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan, and Pakistan and the Sub-Saharan Africa regions, where nearly half and over a third of the population, respectively, are at high risk, and almost everyone who is exposed is also vulnerable.

results.source: Poverty, Prosperity and Planet Report 2026 - Overview.pdf
results.text:
Deprivations extend beyond monetary measures: A deteriorating planet threatens the gains against poverty
Around 4.6 billion people live in exposed areas, and 2.7 billion live in highly vulnerable conditions; about 1.5 billion people experience both types of vulnerability. The drivers of multidimensional poverty also drive climate vulnerability. The same lack of schooling and missing infrastructure that identify a household as multidimensionally poor can convert a flood or a drought from a hazard into a catastrophe.

question: How do the employment rates of working-age adults in poor households compare with those in nonpoor households?

results.source: Poverty, Prosperity and Planet Report 2026 - Overview.pdf
results.text: On employment rates, the poor fall only slightly short of the nonpoor. About three in five working-age adults in poor households are employed, some 6 percentage points below the rate among adults in nonpoor households. Joblessness thus accounts for only part of global poverty. The near parity in employment rates is a global average. The employment gap between the poor and the nonpoor is small or absent in poorer economies and wide in richer economies. It also conceals two shortfalls. Poor workers put in about three to four fewer hours a week relative to nonpoor workers, whether wage earners or self-employed, and the gap is largest in the poorest countries and among the self-employed.

results.source: Poverty, Prosperity and Planet Report 2026 - Overview.pdf
results.text:
Jobs
8. Labor is the main and often only asset of the poor, but their work yields less income per household member than the work of the nonpoor. Working-age adults in poor households are employed at rates only 6 percentage points below the corresponding rates in nonpoor households, but poor workers put in three to four fewer hours a week and support three times as many dependents as workers in the richest households (refer to figure 4, panels a and b). The gap is widening. Employment among the poor fell in 88 of 138 economies over 2003-24, and earnings growth, not employment, delivered all growth in consumption per capita at the bottom of the distribution.

results.source: Poverty, Prosperity and Planet Report 2026 - Overview.pdf
results.text:
Foreword
Jobs are the most direct pathway out of poverty for most households. Poor and nonpoor adults have similar employment rates. One in three adults in poor households are not employed, many of whom are women. Poor workers not only earn less, they also support more dependents. This means that reducing poverty requires both more jobs and better-paying jobs. Expanding employment can make the greatest difference for households living between the $3.00 and $8.30 poverty lines, while raising the earnings of poor workers can have the greatest impact on the poorest households.

results.source: Poverty, Prosperity and Planet Report 2026 - Overview.pdf
results.text:
Concentration is a key fact of global extreme poverty and inequality
This report opens with a sobering projection. If economies grow over the coming years at the per capita economic growth rates experienced from 2015 to 2024, both the global extreme poverty rate and the number of people living in extreme poverty will be higher in 2030 than today. This would not represent a mere pause, but a stunning reversal of the improvement in well-being of the preceding decades. Only sustained annual global economic growth of around 4 percent per capita would bring the global extreme poverty rate down to near the 3 percent target by 2050.

results.text:
Concentration is a key fact of global extreme poverty and inequality
Thus, the global extreme poverty rate would be pulled upward even as the extreme poverty rates in most economies would hold steady or improve. The distinction matters for policy: The challenge is not a diffuse global failure of development, but the clustering of clear needs in an identifiable group of economies.
